Cue words and self-talk

Self-talk is what you say to yourself, aloud or in your head. A cue word is a very short instruction, such as “front edge” or “smooth”, that points your attention at one thing.

In many studies, athletes who practised what to say to themselves did somewhat better. In tasks that need accuracy, short instructions (“front edge”) helped more than encouragement (“come on”). The studies are not from clay shooting, so most likely this works in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting too.

Some research

Tip: Choose two or three short cues with your coach in training. Good cues point at the target or its line: “see it”, “front edge”, “stay on the line”, “finish it”. Keep body cues, such as “elbow up”, for practice sessions.

Coaches' experience

Researchers call this an external focus: paying attention to the target or to where the gun is going, rather than to your own arms and shoulders. Many studies found that it works better. A newer review, which allowed for studies with no effect that often go unpublished, found the average advantage close to zero. So treat cues about the target as a sensible starting point, not a rule.

Some research

Say what to do, not what to avoid. In golf putting studies, players told “don't overshoot” sometimes overshot more, especially when their mind was busy with another task. In another study, such instructions led to over-correction. So try “stay on the line” rather than “don't stop the gun”.

Little research

Motivational phrases such as “come on” or “I can do this” may suit the walk between stands. On the stand, a short instruction usually fits better.

Some research

Use one cue per target and keep the same words in training and in competition. A new cue on the day is like new equipment: try it in training first. You can note your cues in your training diary.

Coaches' experience

Key points

  • Choose 2–3 short cues about the target with your coach.
  • Say what to do, not what to avoid: “stay on the line”, not “don't stop”.
  • Instructions on the stand, motivation between stands.
  • Keep the same cue words in training and in competition.

Did you know?

Many shooters say their cue word at the same step of the routine, just before the call. Then the word itself becomes part of the pre-shot routine.

Stand Talk

  • Coach Front edge.

    Meaning: Look at the front edge of the target, not at the whole clay or the gun.

  • Coach Stay on the line.

    Meaning: Keep the gun moving along the target's flight line.

  • Coach Finish it.

    Meaning: Keep the gun moving after the shot; complete the follow-through.

  • Coach Smooth.

    Meaning: Move the gun calmly and evenly, without a jerk.

For the interpreter
  • Translate the coach's cue the same way each time, in two or three words. If the coach says “front edge”, keep one equivalent for the whole tour, so the shooter can use it as self-talk.
For the coach
  • On the stand, give cues about the target, not about body parts. Keep technical points for practice blocks, not for competition week.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Which cue suits the stand?

    1. Come on, you can do this one
    2. Just don't miss this one again
    3. Front edge, stay on the line
    Answer

    Front edge, stay on the line

    A short instruction about the target fits the stand; motivational phrases suit the walk between stands.

  2. Why can “don't” cues be risky?

    1. They sometimes cause that very error
    2. The referee may count them as coaching
    3. They take too long to say on the stand
    Answer

    They sometimes cause that very error

    In studies, “don't” instructions sometimes caused the error they named, so say what to do instead.

  3. Where do motivational phrases fit better?

    1. On the stand, just before the call
    2. On the walk between stands
    3. During the target presentation
    Answer

    On the walk between stands

    In tasks that need accuracy, short instructions helped more than encouragement, so encouragement fits the time between stands.
